o: Proceedings of the tribes of Judah and Simeon.
bg: judges, book of

Is so called because it contains the history of the deliverance and government of Israel by the men who bore the title of the "judges." The book of Ruth originally formed part of this book, but about A.D. 450 it was separated from it and placed in the Hebrew scriptures immediately after the Song of Solomon.
Jerusalem
It is first mentioned in Scripture under the name Salem (Gen. 14:18; comp. Ps. 76:2). When first mentioned under the name Jerusalem, Adonizedek was its king (Josh. 10:1).
Hebron

The third son of Kohath, who was the second son of Levi. (Exodus 6:18; Numbers 3:19; 1 Chronicles 6:2,18; 23:12) He was the founder of a family of Hebronites, (Numbers 3:27; 26:58; 1 Chronicles 26:23,30,31), or Bene-Hebron. (1 Chronicles 15:9; 23:19) + A city of Judah, (Joshua 15:54) situated among the mountains, (Joshua 20:7) 20 Roman miles south of Jerusalem, and the same distance north of Beersheba.
Simeon
The second of Jacob's son by Leah. His birth is recorded in (Genesis 29:33) The first group of Jacob's children consists, besides Simeon, of the three other sons of Leah--Reuben, Levi, Judah.
ch.s: This chapter covers: Proceedings of the tribes of Judah and Simeon (vv. 1–8); Hebron and other cities taken (vv. 9–20); The proceedings of other tribes (vv. 21–36). People named: Caleb, Simeon, Joseph, Debir, Achsah, Moses. Places: Judah, Jerusalem, Hebron, Kirjath, Perizzites.
ch.mh: The Israelites were convinced that the war against the Canaanites was to be continued; but they were in doubt as to the manner in which it was to be carried on after the death of Joshua.
q: Read verses 1–8 (Proceedings of the tribes of Judah and Simeon). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 9–20 (Hebron and other cities taken), what do you learn about war and conflict?
Verse 7 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Revelation 13:10. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Caleb’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of family and generations in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Judges?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.a: Thank God for His deliverance, and share what He has done for you with one person.

o: The angel of the Lord rebukes the people.
The wickedness of the new generation after Joshua.
bg: judges, book of

Bochim

Weepers, a place where the angel of the Lord reproved the Israelites for entering into a league with the people of the land. This caused them bitterly to weep, and hence the name of the place (Judg. 2:1, 5).
Gaash
A shaking, a hill, on the north side of which Joshua was buried (Josh. 24:30; Judg. 2:9), in the territory of Ephraim. (See TIMNATH-SERAH.)
ch.s: This chapter covers: The angel of the Lord rebukes the people (vv. 1–5); The wickedness of the new generation after Joshua (vv. 6–23). People named: Joshua, Gilgal, Nun, Timnath, Ephraim, Baalim. Places: Bochim, Egypt, Gaash, Ashtaroth.
ch.mh: It was the great Angel of the covenant, the Word, the Son of God, who spake with Divine authority as Jehovah, and now called them to account for their disobedience.
q: Read verses 1–5 (The angel of the Lord rebukes the people). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 6–23 (The wickedness of the new generation after Joshua), what do you learn about family and generations?

What does Joshua’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of idolatry in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Judges?

ch.aq: Let us declare war against every sin, and follow after holiness all our days.
ch.a: Ask God to search your heart, confess what He shows you, and make any right amends.

Lebanon

Lebanon proper, Jebel es-Sharki, commences at its southern extremity in the gorge of the Leontes, the ancient Litany, and extends north-east, parallel to the Mediterranean coast, as far as the river Eleutherus, at the plain of Emesa, "the entering of Hamath" (Num. 34:8; 1 Kings 8:65), in all about 90 geographical miles in extent. The average height of this range is from 6,000 to 8,000 feet; the peak of Jebel Mukhmel
Moab
Used to denote the people of Moab (Num. 22:3-14; Judg. 3:30; 2 Sam. 8:2; Jer. 48:11, 13).
ch.s: This chapter covers: The nations left to prove Israel (vv. 1–7); Othniel delivers Israel (vv. 8–11); Ehud delivers Israel from Eglon (vv. 12–30); Shamgar delivers and judges Israel (vv. 31). ch.mh: As the Israelites were a type of the church on earth, they were not to be idle and slothful.

o: Israel again revolts, and is oppressed by Jabin.
Deborah concerts their deliverance with Barak.
Sisera put to death by Jael.

Harosheth

(workmanship) "of the Gentiles" so called from the mixed races that inhabited it--a city in the north of the land of Canaan, supposed to have stood on the west coast of the lake Merom from which the Jordan issues forth in one unbroken stream. It was the residence of Sisera captain of Jabin king of Canaan, (Judges 4:2) and it was the point to which the victorious Israelites under Barak pursued the discomfited host and
Tabor
A height. (1.) Now Jebel et-Tur, a cone-like prominent mountain, 11 miles west of the Sea of Galilee. It is about 1,843 feet high.
Sisera

(Egypt. Ses-Ra, "servant of Ra"). (1.) The captain of Jabin's army (Judg. 4:2), which was routed and destroyed by the army of Barak on the plain of Esdraelon. After all was lost he fled to the settlement of Heber the Kenite in the plain of Zaanaim.
ch.s: This chapter covers: Israel again revolts, and is oppressed by Jabin (vv. 1–3); Deborah concerts their deliverance with Barak (vv. 4–9); Sisera defeated (vv. 10–16); Sisera put to death by Jael (vv. 17–24). ch.mh: The land had rest for eighty years, which should have confirmed them in their religion; but it made them secure, and indulge their lusts.

In verses 4–9 (Deborah concerts their deliverance with Barak), what do you learn about leadership and kingship?

What does Sisera’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of war and conflict in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Judges?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: When God goes before us in our spiritual conflicts, we must bestir ourselves; and when, by his grace, he gives us some success against the enemies of our souls, we must improve it by watchfulness and resolution.
ch.a: Let the seriousness of God's judgment move you to examine your ways and to pray for others.

o: Praise and glory ascribed to God.
The distress and deliverance of Israel.
bg: judges, book of

Is so called because it contains the history of the deliverance and government of Israel by the men who bore the title of the "judges." The book of Ruth originally formed part of this book, but about A.D. 450 it was separated from it and placed in the Hebrew scriptures immediately after the Song of Solomon.
Kishon

Winding, a winter torrent of Central Palestine, which rises about the roots of Tabor and Gilboa, and passing in a northerly direction through the plains of Esdraelon and Acre, falls into the Mediterranean at the north-eastern corner of the bay of Acre, at the foot of Carmel. It is the drain by which the waters of the plain of Esdraelon and of the mountains that surround it find their way to the sea.
Deborah
A prophetess, "wife" (woman?) of Lapidoth. Jabin, the king of Hazor, had for twenty years held Israel in degrading subjection.
Sisera

(Egypt. Ses-Ra, "servant of Ra"). (1.) The captain of Jabin's army (Judg. 4:2), which was routed and destroyed by the army of Barak on the plain of Esdraelon. After all was lost he fled to the settlement of Heber the Kenite in the plain of Zaanaim.
ch.s: This chapter covers: Praise and glory ascribed to God (vv. 1–5); The distress and deliverance of Israel (vv. 6–11); Some commended, others censured (vv. 12–23); Sisera's mother disappointed (vv. 24–31). People named: Deborah, Sisera, Barak, Abinoam, Jael, Zebulun. Places: Kishon, Seir, Edom, Sinai, Amalek.
ch.mh: No time should be lost in returning thanks to the Lord for his mercies; for our praises are most acceptable, pleasant, and profitable, when they flow from a full heart.

In verses 6–11 (The distress and deliverance of Israel), what do you learn about worship and praise?

What does Deborah’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of war and conflict in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Judges?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let us take heed of indulging eager desires towards any temporal good, particularly toward that which cherishes vain-glory, for that was what she here doted on.
ch.a: Write down three things this chapter shows about God and thank Him for each.

Gaza

Called also Azzah, which is its Hebrew name (Deut. 2:23; 1 Kings 4:24; Jer. 25:20), strong, a city on the Mediterranean shore, remarkable for its early importance as the chief centre of a great commercial traffic with Egypt. It is one of the oldest cities of the world (Gen. 10:19; Josh. 15:47).
Gideon

Called also Jerubbaal (Judg. 6:29, 32), was the first of the judges whose history is circumstantially narrated (Judg. 6-8). His calling is the commencement of the second period in the history of the judges.
Joash
Whom Jehovah bestowed. (1.) A contracted form of Jehoash, the father of Gideon (Judg. 6:11, 29; 8:13, 29, 32).
ch.s: This chapter covers: Israel oppressed by Midianites (vv. 1–6); Israel rebuked by a prophet (vv. 7–10); Gideon set to deliver Israel (vv. 11–24); Gideon destroys Baal's altar (vv. 25–32); Signs given him (vv. 33–40). People named: Gideon, Joash, Abi, Midian, Ophrah, Manasseh. Places: Egypt, Gaza.
ch.mh: Israel's sin was renewed, and Israel's troubles were repeated.

(fear), The well of, a spring by which Gideon and his great army encamped on the morning of the day which ended in the rout of the Midianites. (Judges 7:1) and where the trial of the people by their mode of drinking apparently took place.
Moreh
The plain or plains (or, as it should rather be rendered, the oak or oaks) of Moreh. The oak of Moreh was the first recorded halting-place of Abram after his entrance into the land of Canaan.

Foundation, a place in the open desert wastes on the east of Jordan (Judg. 8:10), not far beyond Succoth and Penuel, to the south. Here Gideon overtook and routed a fugitive band of Midianites under Zeba and Zalmunna, whom he took captive.

A city in Samaria (Gen. 33:18), called also Sichem (12:6), Sychem (Acts 7:16). It stood in the narrow sheltered valley between Ebal on the north and Gerizim on the south, these mountains at their base being only some 500 yards apart.
Thebez

Brightness, a place some 11 miles north-east of Shechem, on the road to Scythopolis, the modern Tabas. Abimelech
A son of Gideon (Judg. 9:1), who was proclaimed king after the death of his father (Judg. 8:33-9:6). One of his first acts was to murder his brothers, seventy in number, "on one stone," at Ophrah.

Arnon

(roaring), the river or torrent which formed the boundary between Moab and the Amorites, on the north of Moab, (Numbers 21:13,14,24,26; Judges 11:22) and afterwards between Moab and Israel (Reuben). (2:24,36; 3:8,12,16; 4:48; Joshua 12:1,2; 13:9,16; Judges 11:13,26) There can be no doubt that the Wady el-Mojeb of the present day is the Arnon. Its principal source is near Katrane, on the Haj route.
Ammon

(sons of renown, mountaineers), Am'monites, Children of Ammon, A people descended from Ben-ammi, the son of Lot by his younger daughter. (Genesis 19:38) comp Psal 83:7,8 The Ammonites are frequently mentioned with the Moabites (descendants of Ben-ammi's half-brother), and sometimes under the same name.

The tribes living on the east of Jordan, separated from their brethren on the west by the deep ravines and the rapid river, gradually came to adopt peculiar customs, and from mixing largely with the Moabites, Ishmaelites, and Ammonites to pronounce certain letters in such a manner as to distinguish them from the other tribes.

Gaza

Called also Azzah, which is its Hebrew name (Deut. 2:23; 1 Kings 4:24; Jer. 25:20), strong, a city on the Mediterranean shore, remarkable for its early importance as the chief centre of a great commercial traffic with Egypt. It is one of the oldest cities of the world (Gen. 10:19; Josh. 15:47).
Hebron

The third son of Kohath, who was the second son of Levi. (Exodus 6:18; Numbers 3:19; 1 Chronicles 6:2,18; 23:12) He was the founder of a family of Hebronites, (Numbers 3:27; 26:58; 1 Chronicles 26:23,30,31), or Bene-Hebron. bg: judges, book of

Shiloh

Shiloh, a place of rest, a city of Ephraim, "on the north side of Bethel," from which it is distant 10 miles (Judg. 21:19); the modern Seilun (the Arabic for Shiloh), a "mass of shapeless ruins." Here the tabernacle was set up after the Conquest (Josh. 18:1-10), where it remained during all the period of the judges till the ark fell into the hands of the Philistines.
Shechem

A city in Samaria (Gen. 33:18), called also Sichem (12:6), Sychem (Acts 7:16). It stood in the narrow sheltered valley between Ebal on the north and Gerizim on the south, these mountains at their base being only some 500 yards apart.
Benjamin
The history of the tribe contains a sad record of a desolating civil war in which they were engaged with the other eleven tribes. By it they were almost exterminated (Judg. 20:20, 21; 21:10).
ch.s: This chapter covers: The Israelites lament for the Benjamites (vv. 1–25). People named: Benjamin, Jabesh, Rimmon. Places: Shiloh, Canaan, Shechem, Lebonah.
ch.mh: Israel lamented for the Benjamites, and were perplexed by the oath they had taken, not to give their daughters to them in marriage.
